items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1975-02-03
items.q: I think that most of the genuine, authentic tendencies in New Orleans jazz came down through Oliver and Louis

ctx.x: That worked certainly. Let's see. We were talking about recording sessions. It was Joe Maera- Mm-hm. He worked with him. Were you working for Joe Maera- Mm-hm.

Not really. What was the basis? No. Let me see what would I say was the basis. Joe, as you know, was very much interested in getting the music of New Orleans recorded. recorded. He has a feeling of commitment about it, the fact that there are a lot of musicians who hadn't been recorded or hadn't been recorded properly. And of course I felt the same way about it, and I always thought of myself as helping out, you know, in many cases proposing and producing sessions myself that I thought were suitable. And so there…
Yeah. Yeah, I'm just wondering how you fit Wiggs into something like this.

items.title: Al Rose Interview, 1976-02-19
items.q: Louis was a unique musical genius who fits into any era, into any style, into any form.

ctx.x: Goodbye. Bye-bye. What I was asking, Al, was that, isn't there a new form of jazz or a new jazz style created in those Hot 5 and Hot 7, which features so predominantly the solo, and not only the solo instrument, but a whole new conception of jazz playing by Louis Armstrong, we'll say.

Well, there are two aspects to what you just raised. One, of course, is the fact that Louis was a unique musical genius who fits into any era, into any style, into any form. And so far as I knew, there was literally nothing that he could not do. So it is very difficult to be able to judge anything that takes place on the basis of Louis' performance, because he was that much of an artist that he virtually transcended everything, anything formal that could have taken place in the 20th century. And it is also true…
